name: La Station
overview: Artist-run contemporary art space and residency in the Halle sud of Le 109, 89 route de Turin, Nice (lastation.org).
Founded in 1996 in Nice and run by the association Starter. It began in a former petrol station at 26 boulevard Gambetta, from which it takes its name (lastation.org).

In October 2009 it moved into the south hall of the former refrigerated warehouses (entrepôts frigorifiques) "mis à disposition par la ville de Nice" (lent by the City of Nice). The renovated premises cover 1,000 m², shared between exhibition spaces and studios, with about a dozen artists working there (lastation.org).
funding_verdict: La Station: self-organised artists' association with public support: DRAC PACA for the residency, and the City of Nice for the premises

name: MAMAC
aliases: Musée d'art moderne et d'art contemporain de Nice
Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Nice
Musée d'Art Moderne et d'Art Contemporain
overview: The City of Nice's museum of modern and contemporary art, at Place Yves Klein next to Place Garibaldi, and one of the city's 11 museums (museum website).
Inaugurated on 21 June 1990 (museum website).

Building: by the architects Yves Bayard and Henri Vidal, four square towers with a red ochre base and Carrara marble surfaces, linked by glass footbridges, built over the covered Paillon river, with ten exhibition rooms and public roof terraces (museum website).
funding_verdict: MAMAC: public: the City of Nice, which owns it and pays for its renovation
wider_context: Nice Premium reported on 30 November 2025 that about a dozen employees of the Magasin in Grenoble described sick leaves, dismissals and disciplinary procedures; eight of eleven employees struck for two hours on 19 November 2025, and unions asked for independent mediation and an organisational audit.

The same article reports that the labour inspectorate refused the dismissal of a staff representative who had reported alleged aggression and sexual harassment, and that management kept up legal action. The article gives the employees' and unions' account only.
The dispute concerns the Magasin, not MAMAC; it is relevant because Kopp now directs MAMAC.

name: Villa Arson
overview: National higher school of art and contemporary art centre at 20 avenue Stephen Liégeard, on the Saint-Barthélemy hill in northern Nice (Villa Arson website; Wikipedia).

The site has the school, the art centre, artist residencies, a publishing shop, a specialist library and Radio Arson; its buildings cover 17,000 m² over five buildings, with 20 residence rooms and 12 studios for artists and researchers (Villa Arson website; activity report 2024 to 2025).

The estate grew around an eighteenth-century villa of the Peyre de La Coste family, bought after the French revolutionary period by the merchant and banker Pierre-Joseph Arson and turned into the Grand Hôtel Saint-Barthélemy at the end of the nineteenth century (Villa Arson website, gardens page).
funding_verdict: Villa Arson: public: a national public establishment under the French Ministry of Culture

name: Lafayette Anticipations
overview: Foundation for contemporary creation at 9 rue du Plâtre in the Marais, Paris, in a building designed by Rem Koolhaas whose mobile floors change the space (foundation website).
Founded by the Groupe Galeries Lafayette, given a public-interest mission in 2012 and opened to the public on 10 March 2018 (foundation website).

What is there: three exhibitions and three festivals a year, among them Échelle Humaine for performance and Closer Music for emerging music, two residency programmes and a production workshop. The collection, held by the Fonds de dotation Famille Moulin, has more than four hundred works; its core is 150 works of the young French scene of the early 2000s from the personal collection of Guillaume Houzé and Ginette Moulin, and an acquisitions committee adds to it each year (foundation website).
funding_verdict: Lafayette Anticipations: private, the Groupe Galeries Lafayette and the Moulin family's endowment fund

name: Musée Jacquemart-André
overview: The Musée Jacquemart-André is a nineteenth-century mansion at 158 Boulevard Haussmann, built to designs by Henri Parent between 1869 and 1876 (museum website).

Édouard André began collecting in 1860; after his death in 1894 his wife Nélie Jacquemart continued, died on 15 May 1912 and left the mansion to the Institut de France; the museum opened on 8 December 1913 (museum website).

What is there: Italian Renaissance, Flemish and eighteenth-century French works, goldsmiths' work, ceramics, tapestries, Delacroix, Orientalist and Barbizon paintings, portraits by Winterhalter, a Tiepolo ceiling in the dining room and Paolo Uccello's Saint George (museum website; The Art Newspaper France, 14 September 2023). The pages read give no total number of works.
funding_verdict: Musée Jacquemart-André: owned by the Institut de France, run by the private operator Culturespaces, financing not detailed

name: Musée des Augustins
aliases: Augustins, musée des beaux-arts de Toulouse
overview: The Musée des Augustins is in the Augustinian convent, with the only fourteenth-century cloister of the south-west preserved in full, at 21 rue de Metz (press kit, December 2025).
The convent became national property in the Revolution, was closed in 1790, and the Museum du Midi de la République opened there in 1795, two years after the Louvre (press kit).

What is there: about 4,000 works in the collection (press kit) and 3,900 records in the online collections database (museum website). Works run from the medieval period, with Romanesque sculpture and Toulouse Renaissance painting, to the early twentieth century.
funding_verdict: Musée des Augustins: municipal, with small State and Region grants and a public appeal for the cloister

name: MAC VAL
overview: Departmental museum of contemporary art on place de la Libération in Vitry-sur-Seine, south-east of Paris (Centre Pompidou partner page; InventCulture case study, 2023).

The Val-de-Marne department began supporting contemporary creation in 1982; a curator's post was created in 1998 and Alexia Fabre recruited; construction began in 2002 and the museum opened in November 2005. Fabre left for the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in 2022 and Nicolas Surlapierre succeeded her on 3 October 2022 (InventCulture case study, 2023; franceinfo; Le Quotidien de l'Art).
What is there: a collection of art in France from the 1950s on, begun by the department in 1982, which counted 2,000 works ten years after the opening (franceinfo, 2015).
funding_verdict: MAC VAL: public, the Val-de-Marne department; state and region shared the building cost

name: Museum Frieder Burda
overview: The Museum Frieder Burda is a museum of modern and contemporary art on Lichtentaler Allee 8b, Baden-Baden, in a building by the American architect Richard Meier (museum website).

The Stiftung Frieder Burda was established on 20 April 1998; the museum opened on 22 October 2004 and sits next to the state-run Staatliche Kunsthalle Baden-Baden, connected by a glass bridge (museum website).

What is there: about 1,000 works of classical modernism and contemporary art, paintings, sculptures, objects, photographs and works on paper, collected by Frieder Burda, whose collection began in 1968 with a painting by Lucio Fontana (museum website).
funding_verdict: Museum Frieder Burda: private foundation of its collector-founder; income not stated on the pages read

name: KINDL Centre for Contemporary Art
overview: KINDL is a centre for contemporary art at Am Sudhaus 3, Neukölln, in the former Kindl brewery, built between 1926 and 1930 by the architects Hans Claus and Richard Schepke in the Expressionist style (KINDL website).

Salome Grisard and Burkhard Varnholt bought the complex in 2011 and had it converted; exhibitions have run since 2016. Founding director Andreas Fiedler led it until Kathrin Becker took over artistic direction in February 2020 (KINDL website, institution page).

What is there: temporary exhibitions in the Sudhaus, whose six copper brewing kettles were then the largest in Europe; the pages read describe no permanent collection (KINDL website). Current shows include Mischa Kuball, Kira Freije and Thu-Van Tran, running into 2027.
funding_verdict: KINDL: privately founded nonprofit; named funders not on the pages read.

name: Kunstraum Kreuzberg/Bethanien
overview: Municipal gallery for group and thematic exhibitions on contemporary social and cultural issues, at Mariannenplatz 2 in Kreuzberg, Berlin. The nearest U-Bahn station is Kottbusser Tor, with bus 140 to Mariannenplatz.

Founded in 1973 in the former operating rooms of the Bethanien deaconess hospital, which closed in 1970 and was slated for demolition. The fight to save it became a starting point of Kreuzberg's alternative culture and squatter scene (taz interview with Stéphane Bauer, 27 September 2023). It was called Kunstamt Kreuzberg/Bethanien until 2001 (Wikipedia).
The building is the former Diakonissen-Krankenhaus, built in 1847 to designs by Theodor von Stein. Since summer 2010 it has been called Kunstquartier Bethanien (stated by the space).
funding_verdict: Kunstraum Kreuzberg/Bethanien: the Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg district, with Berlin Senate exhibition funding and project grants

name: Josef Albers Museum Quadrat
overview: The Josef Albers Museum Quadrat is part of the Museumszentrum Quadrat on the edge of the Stadtgarten in Bottrop (bigbeautifulbuildings.de).
The original complex opened in 1976; Josef Albers, born in Bottrop in 1888, was made an honorary citizen in 1970 and gave prints and pictures to the city (bigbeautifulbuildings.de).

What is there: the Albers collection, which includes the series Homage to the Square. Albers died in 1976, and in 1979 his wife transferred more than 300 of his works to the collection, which led to an expansion completed in 1981 to 1983 (bigbeautifulbuildings.de). In 2016 the museum bought 28 photographs and photomontages by Albers from the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation in Connecticut (land.nrw, 21 September 2016).
funding_verdict: Josef Albers Museum Quadrat: municipal, with foundation and Land money for purchases; amounts not stated on the pages read

name: Kolumba
aliases: Art Museum of the Archdiocese of Cologne
overview: Kolumba is the art museum of the Archdiocese of Cologne, in a building that combines a ruined church with modern architecture (museum website).
It was founded in 1853 as the Diocesan Museum of Cologne, was renamed Kolumba in 2004, and the new building by the Swiss architect Peter Zumthor opened on 15 September 2007 (museen.koeln).

What is there: a collection from late antiquity to the present day, shown mostly from the museum's own holdings with a new selection each year on 15 September, without object labels and without separating works by period, style or medium. The pages read gave no object count (museen.koeln).
funding_verdict: Kolumba: church-run, operated by the Archdiocese of Cologne; budget not stated on the pages read

name: Museum Ostwall
overview: Museum Ostwall occupies the fourth and fifth floors of the Dortmunder U in Dortmund, with temporary exhibitions on the sixth (Ruhr Tourismus).

It was founded after the war with a focus on Classical Modernism, against the Nazi 'degenerate art' label; its founder is given as Leonie Reygers (Ruhr Tourismus). The pages read did not give the opening year.

What is there: a permanent display focused on Fluxus, with Joseph Beuys, Allan Kaprow, Dieter Roth and Wolf Vostell, and a path back through New Objectivity, Informel, ZERO and Classical Modernism; works by the Brücke and Blue Rider groups, and a large Alexej von Jawlensky collection (Ruhr Tourismus). Revierpassagen named Christian Rohlfs's Clowngespräch (1912), August Macke's Großer Zoologischer Garten (1913) and Vostell's TEK (1970) (Revierpassagen, 10 November 2017). The pages read gave no object count.
funding_verdict: Museum Ostwall: municipal, City of Dortmund; funding not stated on the pages read

name: Museum Küppersmühle für Moderne Kunst (MKM)
overview: The MKM Museum Küppersmühle für Moderne Kunst is in a 19th century mill in Duisburg's Inner Harbour that worked as a mill until 1972 (museum website).
The mill was converted into a museum in 1999; Herzog & de Meuron designed the extension completed in 2021, which brought the exhibition space to about 6,100 m2 (museum website).

What is there: the Ströher Collection of German art after 1945, mainly painting, on more than 5,000 m2, with more than 300 works from the 1950s onward by artists including Anselm Kiefer, Gerhard Richter and Pierre Soulages (museum website). The Haniel Collection show 'Show Your Colors!' runs on the third floor from 8 October 2026 for one year (museum website).
funding_verdict: MKM: private collector foundation and a non-profit association; amounts not stated on the pages read

name: Ruhr Museum
overview: The Ruhr Museum is in the former coal washing plant of Zollverein colliery, Shaft XII, in Essen, and presents the natural and cultural history of the Ruhr area (museum website).

It has existed since 1 January 2008 as a dependent foundation within the Zollverein Foundation; its collections are largely those of the former Ruhrlandmuseum of the city of Essen (museum website, about us).

What is there: natural history, archaeology, history and photography collections; 25,000 selected items can be seen on tours of the display depot at the Zollverein Coking Plant (museum website). The pages read gave no total.
funding_verdict: Ruhr Museum: public, the state, the city of Essen and the Landschaftsverband Rheinland.

name: Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt
aliases: SCHIRN KUNSTHALLE FRANKFURT am Main GmbH
overview: An exhibition hall for modern and contemporary art in Frankfurt am Main, showing since September 2025 in the former Dondorf printing works in Bockenheim while its building on the Römerberg is renovated (hessenschau, 6 September 2025).

The Römerberg building dates from 1986 (entwicklungsstadt.de, 9 February 2026) and the Schirn says it has been making exhibitions for nearly 40 years (Schirn website); the operator is SCHIRN KUNSTHALLE FRANKFURT am Main GmbH, director Sebastian Baden (imprint).
The pages read describe temporary exhibitions and name no permanent collection; the Bockenheim site has 900 square metres of exhibition space in two halls (hessenschau, 6 September 2025).
funding_verdict: Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt: mainly public, a city-owned company, plus partners and sponsors it does not name on the pages read

name: basis Frankfurt
overview: Production and exhibition platform and studio house at Gutleutstraße 8-12 in the Bahnhofsviertel, Frankfurt (Journal Frankfurt).
The association basis e.V. has run the studio house there since 2007, with low-cost workspaces and a support programme for young artists (Journal Frankfurt).
Artistic directors named in 2016: Felix Ruhöfer and Jakob Sturm (Journal Frankfurt).
funding_verdict: basis Frankfurt: mainly public: City of Frankfurt and the state of Hesse

name: Zeppelin Museum
overview: The Zeppelin Museum is at Seestraße 22, Friedrichshafen (museum website).
The pages read did not give its founder, founding year or collection.
What is there: the pages read did not describe the collection or give a count.
funding_verdict: Zeppelin Museum: city subsidy of a museum company; recent figures not stated on the pages read

name: Thalia Theater
overview: The Thalia Theater is one of Hamburg's four Staatstheater, at Alstertor in the city centre, with a main house of about 1,000 seats and a studio in the Gaußstraße in Altona with 200 (theatre website; hamburg.de).
Chéri Maurice opened it in 1843; a new building with 1,300 seats followed in 1912, it was nationalised in 1937, destroyed in 1945 and reopened restored in 1960 (theatre website; hamburg.de).
What is there: an ensemble of 36 actors, about 350 permanent staff, about 20 premieres a season and about 850 events a year for roughly 250,000 visitors (theatre website).
funding_verdict: Thalia Theater: public, owned by the city of Hamburg; subsidy amounts not stated on the pages read

name: Museum Würth
overview: Museum Würth is one of the art venues of the Würth Group, which makes fastening and assembly technology and has its headquarters in Künzelsau-Gaisbach (Schwäbische Zeitung, 17 June 2026).

Reinhold Würth built the collection; the German houses are Hirschwertscheuer in Künzelsau (1989), Museum Würth in Künzelsau-Gaisbach (1991), Kunsthalle Würth in Schwäbisch Hall (2001), the Johanniterkirche in Schwäbisch Hall (2008) and Museum Würth 2 in Künzelsau (2020, by David Chipperfield, with a concert hall) (Schwäbische Zeitung, 17 June 2026).

What is there: the Sammlung Würth spans about 500 years from the late Middle Ages to the 21st century with more than 20,000 works, shaped by Würth's personal interests (Schwäbische Zeitung, 17 June 2026); the Stuttgarter Zeitung quotes the collection's growth from 500 to 21,000 works (Stuttgarter Zeitung, interview with Maria Würth).
funding_verdict: Würth museums: corporate, paid by the Würth Group; no budget stated
